CURRENT PHASE: ios_architecture_review
PHASE PURPOSE: Review the app as an iOS product before final tech specs: SwiftUI architecture, Apple framework choices, local persistence, privacy, permissions, offline behavior, StoreKit/subscription architecture, permissive dependency policy, and testability.

===== ORIGINAL PROMPT (initial_prompt.md) =====
Design and build a complex, production-shaped native iOS app that requires a
real server-side backend (not local-only, not a static/offline app) — pick a
genuinely creative, non-obvious idea that solves a real, specific pain point
well enough that it has a real shot at organic/viral growth. Do not default
to another todo-list, habit-tracker, journaling, or AI-wrapper app — those
categories are saturated and none of them are "unique." Think harder for an
underserved, emotionally sticky, inherently-social-or-real-time problem
where a mobile client + backend architecture is actually necessary (real-time
sync across users/devices, a shared/live data feed, matching or coordination
between people, server-side processing too heavy for on-device, etc.) — the
backend requirement should come from the idea being genuinely multi-user or
real-time, not be bolted on.

Requirements for the idea itself (spend real effort on this — the idea is
the deliverable, not just the code):
- Solves one specific, sharply-defined pain point for a specific audience
  (not "everyone"). Be able to state the pain point and audience in one
  sentence each.
- Has a natural viral/sharing loop baked into the core mechanic — not a
  bolted-on "invite friends" button, but something where using the app is
  inherently more valuable or fun with other people, or naturally produces
  something worth sharing outside the app.
- Genuinely requires a backend: real-time multiplayer/sync, a live shared
  feed, server-side matching/aggregation, push notifications driven by
  server-side events, or similar — justify the architecture choice.
- Is creative enough that a stranger hearing the one-line pitch would say
  "oh that's clever" rather than "isn't that just [existing app]?"

Technical scope:
- Native iOS client (SwiftUI).
- A real backend service (your choice of stack — pick something sensible
  and justify it) handling auth, data sync/storage, and whatever real-time
  or server-side logic the concept needs.
- Design the API contract, data model, and sync/real-time strategy properly
  before building — this is a "complicated app," not an MVP toy.
- Production-shaped: reasonable auth flow, error handling, loading/empty/
  offline states, and a coherent onboarding funnel a real user could follow.
- Visual design should be distinctive and match the concept — not generic
  default SwiftUI styling — but the primary bar for this app is the idea,
  the architecture, and it actually working end-to-end (client <-> backend).

Start by proposing and committing to the specific concept (pain point,
audience, viral loop, and why it needs a backend) before moving into specs
and build, and carry that concept consistently through naming, design, and
onboarding copy.

Let me put this together as a complete client-architecture-first pass at the design spec, since nobody's spoken yet this phase.

I want to start from the thing that will actually break if we get it wrong: how the client learns about state changes it didn't cause. The push notification payload must never be treated as data — Apple doesn't guarantee delivery order, a payload can arrive stale or duplicated, and treating it as truth would recreate exactly the false-confidence failure this whole app exists to eliminate. The correct pattern is: push arrival is a wake-up signal only, which triggers a targeted GET on that specific request, and the UI transitions only after that authoritative fetch resolves. That means every BeaconCard transition — whether caused by this device's own tap or a push-triggered refetch — goes through the same single reconciliation path into view state, which also means "awaiting-confirmation" (my own action, in flight) and "reconciling" (someone else's action, just learned about) can share the identical pulse visual but need to be distinct internal states, because if we collapse them a build agent will wire the reconcile path to skip the pulse and jump straight to the terminal card, which breaks the demo's whole point of watching both phones resolve in real time. I'd also add a client-side foreground refresh — on scenePhase becoming active, refetch the board — as a backstop for the honestly-documented case where APNs silently drops a push on a fresh pod's first incident; this isn't a websocket, it's a cheap correctness net, and it should not be confused with the still-open elapsed timer, which should tick locally off a stored server timestamp so we're not hammering the network just to advance a clock.

Two data-model consequences fall out of the multi-open-request decision that I don't think anyone's pinned down yet. First, ordering: if a pod can have two simultaneously open requests, the board needs a server-defined, stable sort (I'd propose oldest-created-first, since age is already the thing we're surfacing as the urgency signal) and the client must render server order verbatim rather than re-sorting locally — otherwise two devices with slightly different fetch timing show cards in different positions, which is a subtle but real ambiguity bug in an app whose entire premise is zero ambiguity. **Claude (Frontend Engineer · Systems Thinker) — Round 2**

But I want to push back hard on one specific thing in your palette before we lock it, because I don't think it's a stylistic quibble, I think it actually contradicts something the design_discussion phase already fought about and settled. Your neutrals — background `#F3F7FB`, surface.strong `#EAF0F7`, dark surface `#171E29` — all lean blue. That's exactly the "cold blue-black sci-fi/military HUD" register that got explicitly named and rejected in DEC-design_discussion-001, specifically because it makes the app read as alarming rather than calm-under-stress for a parent who's just realized they can't make pickup. Your state colors (the amber pulse, the teal confirmed) are fine and match what was locked — it's the neutral scaffolding underneath them that's quietly reintroducing the tone everyone agreed to avoid. I'd rather we warm those specific tokens — something like a warm off-white background instead of a blue-white, warm charcoal instead of blue-black for dark mode — while keeping everything else in your palette, your type scale, your spacing, and your radii exactly as you wrote them. This isn't me trying to win back my own hex values, it's flagging that we're about to ship a token file that technically satisfies "distinctive palette with light/dark hex" while quietly violating a decision that was actually argued over and locked two phases ago.

Second thing: your Relay Board active-state spec says cards are "sorted by urgency then age." I don't think we have an urgency field anywhere — go back through every decision from initial_discussion through app_features and there's no priority/severity/urgency tier on a request, just requester, note, and timestamps. If we write "urgency" into the formal spec without defining what it means or where it comes from, we're doing exactly the thing the phase rules explicitly forbid — "no adjective may stand in for a number" — and we're handing the build agent an undefined sort key it'll either invent arbitrarily or silently drop. I'd rather we just commit to what the data actually supports: sort by created-at ascending, oldest-and-therefore-most-aged request first, server-authoritative order, and the client renders it verbatim rather than re-sorting locally. That was my point from round one and I don't think anything in your spec actually disagrees with it, it just accidentally introduced a field that doesn't exist. If someone genuinely wants an urgency concept later, that's a real feature proposal for a future phase, not something to smuggle into a sort-order clause here.

Now the part I think matters most and where I want to be really explicit: your per-screen spec is thorough on states, but it's silent on how the client actually learns those states changed, and that silence is exactly where a build agent will take the shortcut that breaks the demo. Nothing in your spec says "don't trust the push payload" — and if that's not written down as an explicit rule, the fast, obvious implementation path for any competent iOS engineer is to decode the notification's userInfo dictionary and update the card directly from it, because that's less code than triggering a fetch. That's the bug I'm most worried about in this entire build, more than any color choice, because it would pass every screenshot review and even pass a casual demo, and then quietly fail the actual race-condition guarantee the whole app exists to prove, the first time APNs delivers two pushes out of order or drops one. I want this written into the spec as a hard architectural rule sitting alongside your interaction invariants: push notification arrival triggers an authoritative refetch of that specific request; the card only transitions after that fetch resolves; the payload itself is never rendered as state. And I want your Request Detail state list to explicitly carry the distinction I raised last round between "awaiting acceptance/accept ack" (this device's own action, mid-flight) and a second state for "I just learned the server already resolved this via someone else's action" — call it `reconciling` if you want a name for it — because if those two get collapsed into one internal case, the most likely implementation is that the losing device just snaps straight to "already covered" with no pulse at all, which kills the exact visual proof the two-phone demo is built around: both screens doing the same calm animation, one locking one way, one locking the other.

Same logic applies to two more states you didn't include that I don't think we can drop: `queuedOffline` for an action taken with no connection (visually and textually distinct from "awaiting confirmation" — one says "we're mid-round-trip right now," the other says "this hasn't left the device yet"), and a specific "this request is no longer open" state for a push deep-link that resolves to a request that's since been withdrawn or expired — that's going to happen constantly given how this app is actually used, someone taps a notification thirty seconds after the thing got handled, and if we don't name that state explicitly it'll get rendered as a generic error, which is scary and wrong for something that's actually a fine outcome. And since we're talking about relaunch behavior — R-018's force-quit-mid-accept test needs a home in this spec too. Cached data should render instantly on cold launch, per the local-first read rule everyone's agreed to, but it needs a subtle board-level "syncing" indicator — not per-card, a single top-level one — that persists until the first fresh fetch of that session actually lands, so a user who force-quit during a mid-flight accept doesn't see week-old cached state presented with the same confidence as fresh state.

Two small things and then I'll land on the Claude Design question. Your ElapsedTimerLabel spec says HH:MM:SS — I think that's the wrong format for what's actually a same-day, usually-sub-hour window; I'd rather it read MM:SS while under an hour and roll to "Xh Ym" past that, both because "00:14:32" is visually noisier in a small chip than it needs to be and because leading zeros on an hours field that's almost always zero is just wasted legibility. And I'd merge my ConnectionBanner idea into your SessionHintBanner rather than propose a separate component — but I want it explicit that the banner needs at least two distinct copy states under one component, "you're offline, your actions are queued" versus "connection's shaky, some pod members may not have gotten this yet," because those are different facts a user needs to act on differently and collapsing them into one vague "connection issue" string undermines the honest-delivery-count requirement we already locked as demo-critical.

On Claude Design: I said no external pass, you offered an optional prompt. I want to just close this instead of leaving two soft answers on the table — my actual reasoning is that the entire value of this design system lives in a state machine (the pulse, the latch, the parity between winner and loser), and a static mockup tool literally cannot represent that; the risk isn't "we don't have a design pass," it's "we get a gorgeous set of frames that can't prove the one thing this app is actually judged on, and someone mistakes polished statics for a validated interaction." **DESIGN SPEC - Core state machine:** every request card is one of `openUnclaimed`, `awaitingConfirmation` (own action in flight), `queuedOffline` (action stored locally, not yet in-flight), `reconciling` (device didn't initiate this change — push wake triggered an authoritative refetch), `latchedConfirmed`, `latchedAlreadyCovered`, `reopened`, `stillOpen`, `withdrawn`, `completed`, `error`. `latchedConfirmed` and `latchedAlreadyCovered` share identical pulse→latch motion/duration. Board ordering is server-authoritative `displayOrder` (created-at ascending + backend tie-break) — no urgency field exists, no client-side re-sort, ever.

**DESIGN SPEC - Push/sync architecture rule (non-negotiable):** push payloads are never rendered as state. A push is a wake-up signal only; it triggers a targeted authoritative refetch of that request, and the card transitions only once that fetch resolves. On launch/foreground and after a force-quit mid-action, show a single top-level "Syncing latest pod state…" banner (not per-card) until the first fresh fetch of the session lands; stale cache still renders underneath for continuity, but no terminal card is shown with full confidence before that first sync completes.

**DESIGN SPEC - Per-screen states:**
- *AuthGate*: signed-out ready (Apple Sign-In CTA) · signing-in loading (disabled UI, "Checking sign-in…") · error with inline banner + retry · success routes by session token.
- *PodOnboarding*: podless empty ("You're not in a pod yet" + Create pod / Join with code) · create/join in-progress (disabled, honest copy, no fake success) · invalid/expired code error + retry · success routes only after server ack.
- *RelayBoard*: all-clear pod-of-one (pod name, member count, "Share the invite") · all-clear populated ("No active requests" + Post CTA) · active stack (BeaconCards in server `displayOrder`) · loading shimmer · syncing banner · error banner + retry, never blank.
- *RequestComposer*: edit (note + optional short note, no child fields) · queuedOffline · awaitingConfirmation (disabled inputs) · success only on ack · failed + retry, no optimistic post.
- *RequestDetail*: open/unclaimed with visible timer + accept CTA · awaitingConfirmation / queuedOffline / reconciling (each distinct) · latchedConfirmed / latchedAlreadyCovered (identical motion, no red/shake/alert icon on loser) · reopened · stillOpen + re-broadcast · withdrawn (requester-only, muted slate, no receipt) · completed (muted slate + receipt action) · error + retry. Deep-link entry has 3 branches: `alreadySynced` (render immediately), `syncing` (spinner), `noLongerOpen` (respectful close copy, no alarm tone/icon — this will happen routinely).
- *Receipt*: loading · loaded (internal + masked share projection, "Former member" placeholders for deleted accounts) · unavailable + reload.
- *Profile* / *PodSettings*: plain, token-driven, zero custom transitions/motion/illustration; PodSettings has code chip + revoke/reissue with its own error+retry.

**DESIGN SPEC - Motion & haptics:** open→awaiting pulse: scale 0.99→1.02 + border alpha oscillation, 0.9s ease-in-out, repeating. Resolution latch (winner or loser, identical): 0.45s spring, response 0.45, damping 0.82 — no shake, no alert icon, no red on the loser. Reduce Motion collapses both to a ~0.15s crossfade, preserving all text/icon state changes. Haptics: neutral/soft on server-confirmed landing for both winner and loser — never a warning/error haptic for "already covered." Elapsed-timer format: MM:SS under one hour, then "Xh Ym."

**DESIGN SPEC - Accessibility:** every icon-only control has an explicit VoiceOver label + hint; each card reads as one composed sentence ("Request from {member}, status {status}, elapsed {time}, {available action}"); color never carries state alone — every chip pairs icon + text; 44×44 minimum hit targets; Dynamic Type reflows to a vertical stack at AX3–AX5 rather than clipping/truncating; AA contrast against all semantic surfaces in both appearances; connection/session banner carries two distinct copies (offline-with-queued-actions vs. uncertain-delivery) rather than one vague string.

**Craft-budget priority under time pressure:** (1) open→awaiting pulse, (2) winner/loser latch, (3) completed/withdrawn terminal clarity — everything else, including the resting state and secondary screens, stays plain and correct.

**Claude Design:** not used for this build. The spec above is implemented directly in SwiftUI; the previously drafted upload prompt is kept on file only as a future static-asset fallback (e.g. App Store imagery), generated after interaction implementation is complete, never before.

# Testing & Quality for a Small iOS App

Target: **iOS 17+ deployment / Swift 5.9+**, built with **Xcode 16 or later** (Swift Testing ships in-box; use `OS=latest` in CI so the simulator version tracks your toolchain). Zero third-party deps — everything here is Apple first-party. This is a pragmatic reference for an AI building a prototype: maximize confidence per line of test code, avoid brittle tests that break on every UI tweak.

---

## TL;DR strategy for a prototype

- **Don't chase coverage.** Test the code that would be embarrassing or expensive if wrong: money math, date logic, parsing, persistence round-trips, state machines, reducers/view models.
- **Skip testing SwiftUI view bodies.** Use **Xcode Previews** as your visual feedback loop instead — they are faster than any UI test.
- **Make logic testable by moving it out of views** into plain `struct`/`class` types with injected dependencies. If it's testable, it's usually also better architected.
- **One happy-path UI test** through the primary flow catches wiring/regression bugs that unit tests can't. More than a handful of UI tests is usually a net negative for a prototype (slow, flaky).
- **Prefer Swift Testing (`@Test`)** for new unit tests. Keep XCTest for **UI tests** (`XCUIApplication`) and **performance tests** (`measure`) — those APIs are XCTest-only.

Priority order to write tests, highest first:
1. Pure logic with branches (pricing, validation, formatting, sorting/filtering).
2. View model / reducer state transitions (given input → expected observable state).
3. Persistence & serialization round-trips (Codable, SwiftData/UserDefaults).
4. Networking mappers (raw JSON → domain model), with a fake session — never hit the real network.
5. One end-to-end UI smoke test of the core flow.

---

## Project setup

- **Unit test target**: File ▸ New ▸ Target ▸ *Unit Testing Bundle*. Choose **Swift Testing** (default in Xcode 16+) or XCTest.
- **UI test target**: separate *UI Testing Bundle* — it launches the app as a black box.
- Add app code to tests with `@testable import YourApp` (unit tests only; gives access to `internal` symbols). UI tests use the accessibility layer, not imports.
- A `.xctestplan` lets you group tests, set env vars, and pick run configurations (e.g. randomized order). One default plan is fine for a prototype.
- Swift Testing and XCTest **coexist in the same target and same run** — migrate incrementally.

## Swift Testing (`@Test`) — the modern default

Import `Testing`, not `XCTest`. Tests are global functions or methods annotated `@Test`; assertions use `#expect` (non-fatal, keeps going) and `#require` (fatal, unwraps/stops).

```swift
import Testing
@testable import MyApp

@Test func totalIncludesTax() {
    let cart = Cart(items: [.init(price: 10), .init(price: 5)])
    #expect(cart.total(taxRate: 0.1) == 16.5)
}
```

- `#expect(expr)` records a failure and **continues** — the macro captures sub-expression values, so a failure prints the actual operands (no need for XCTest-style messages).
- `#require(expr)` throws and **halts the test** on failure — use it for preconditions where continuing is pointless. It also unwraps optionals (call in a `throws` test with `try`):

```swift
@Test func parsesUser() throws {
    let user = try #require(User(json: validJSON))  // stops here if nil
    #expect(user.name == "Ada")
}
```

### Suites and shared setup

Group with a `struct` (preferred) or `final class`. A **fresh instance is created per test**, so `init` is your per-test setup — no shared mutable state between tests by default.

```swift
@Suite("Cart pricing")
struct CartTests {
    let cart: Cart              // built fresh for every @Test below

    init() { cart = Cart(items: [.init(price: 10)]) }

    @Test func emptyTaxIsIdentity() {
        #expect(cart.total(taxRate: 0) == 10)
    }
}
```

Teardown: for a `struct` suite there usually is none — value types just drop when the instance goes away. If you genuinely need cleanup, use a `final class` and put it in `deinit`. Note `deinit` **cannot be `async` or `throwing`** and can't be actor-isolated, so for `@MainActor` suites or async cleanup, do the work at the end of each test (or use a custom scoping trait) rather than relying on `deinit`.

### Parameterized tests — one test, many cases

Replaces copy-pasted test bodies. Each argument runs as a **separate, independently-reported case**. A single array of tuples destructures positionally into multiple parameters:

```swift
@Test(arguments: [
    ("", false),
    ("a@b.co", true),
    ("no-at", false),
])
func validatesEmail(_ input: String, _ expected: Bool) {
    #expect(EmailValidator.isValid(input) == expected)
}
```

Destructuring is positional — element labels in the tuples don't have to match parameter names and are best omitted to avoid confusion. Cross-product of two sequences (every combination):

```swift
@Test(arguments: [1, 2, 3], ["x", "y"])   // 6 cases
func combos(n: Int, s: String) { #expect(!s.isEmpty && n > 0) }
```

Wrap in `zip(a, b)` when you want **paired** (not cross-product) cases:

```swift
@Test(arguments: zip([1, 2, 3], ["a", "b", "c"]))   // 3 cases
func paired(n: Int, s: String) { #expect(n > 0 && !s.isEmpty) }
```

### Traits: naming, tagging, skipping, known bugs

```swift
@Test("Discount never goes negative")                       // display name
@Test(.disabled("flaky until CI fix"))                      // skip, stays visible
@Test(.enabled(if: FeatureFlags.checkoutV2))                // conditional run
@Test(.bug("https://example.com/issue/42", "rounding"))     // url first, then title
@Test(.tags(.fast))                                         // group across files
```

Define tags once (do **not** add `@Test` — a tag is not a test):

```swift
extension Tag { @Tag static var fast: Self }
```

Run a subset from the CLI with `swift test --filter` / `xcodebuild ... -only-testing:`, or filter by tag in Xcode's Test navigator.
